stem: The chapter 'Rebels and the Raj' deals with which major event in Indian history?
solution: The chapter deals with the Revolt of 1857 (also called the Rebellion of 1857, the Sepoy Mutiny, or the First War of Independence) — the great uprising against British/East India Company rule that began in 1857. It examines how the revolt spread, who took part, its causes, the visions of the rebels, and how the events have been represented in various sources and images. So the event is the Revolt of 1857.

stem: The Revolt of 1857 began with the uprising of the sepoys (Indian soldiers of the Company's army) at __________ on 10 May 1857.
solution: The Revolt of 1857 broke out with the mutiny of the sepoys at Meerut on 10 May 1857. The sepoys there rose up, released imprisoned comrades, killed several British officers, and then marched to Delhi. So the immediate outbreak was at Meerut on 10 May 1857. (Earlier, in late March 1857, Mangal Pandey had revolted at Barrackpore, an important precursor.)

stem: After rising at Meerut, the sepoys marched to Delhi and proclaimed the aged Mughal emperor __________ as their leader/symbolic head.
solution: After the Meerut outbreak, the sepoys marched to Delhi (on 11 May 1857) and rallied around the aged Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar (Bahadur Shah II), proclaiming him as their leader and the symbolic head of the revolt. This gave the rebellion a legitimacy and a unifying symbol — the restoration of Mughal authority. Bahadur Shah, though reluctant and largely powerless, lent his name to the uprising. So the emperor proclaimed as leader was Bahadur Shah Zafar. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The immediate spark that ignited the sepoys' anger in 1857 was the introduction of the new __________.
options: Enfield rifle cartridges, rumoured to be greased with the fat of cows and pigs (offending both Hindu and Muslim sepoys)
solution: The immediate spark of the 1857 Revolt was the introduction of the new Enfield rifle and its cartridges. The cartridges had to be bitten open before loading, and a rumour spread that they were GREASED with the fat of COWS (sacred to Hindus) and PIGS (taboo to Muslims). This deeply OFFENDED the religious sentiments of both Hindu and Muslim sepoys, who saw it as a British plot to defile their religion and force conversion. This grievance ignited the mutiny. So the immediate cause was the greased cartridge affair. (It was, however, only the spark; deeper causes underlay the revolt.)

stem: The sepoy who is famous for an early act of defiance at Barrackpore in March 1857 (attacking his officers), and who was executed, was __________.
solution: Mangal Pandey was a sepoy at Barrackpore (near Calcutta) who, in late March 1857, revolted — attacking his British officers — in an early act of defiance connected with the discontent over the cartridges. He was court-martialled and executed (hanged). His act is often seen as a precursor/harbinger of the wider revolt that broke out at Meerut a few weeks later. So the sepoy at Barrackpore was Mangal Pandey. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The revolt was not confined to the sepoys; it became a broad uprising as many __________ joined it.
options: Peasants, artisans, taluqdars/landholders, and ordinary people (especially in North India) joined the sepoys
Only Mughal princes joined, and no one else
solution: The Revolt of 1857 was not merely a military mutiny; in many areas it broadened into a POPULAR uprising as large numbers of civilians joined the rebel sepoys. Peasants, artisans, dispossessed taluqdars and landholders (especially in Awadh), religious figures, and other ordinary people took part — attacking symbols of British authority, moneylenders, and record offices. This popular participation (particularly across North India — the Gangetic plain and central India) gave the revolt its wide scope and intensity. So peasants, artisans, taluqdars, and ordinary people joined it. This broad social base is an important point.

stem: The region where the revolt was especially intense and had deep popular roots, partly because of resentment at the recent British annexation and the grievances of the taluqdars and peasants, was __________.
solution: The revolt was especially intense and deeply rooted in AWADH (Oudh). Awadh had been recently ANNEXED by the British (in 1856, under the Doctrine of Lapse/on grounds of 'misgovernment', deposing the Nawab Wajid Ali Shah), which caused widespread resentment. The dispossession and reduced status of the TALUQDARS (the powerful local landholders), the disruption of the old social order and patronage networks, the grievances of the PEASANTS under the new revenue arrangements, and the wounded pride at the removal of the popular Nawab all combined to make Awadh a centre of fierce and popular rebellion. So the region was Awadh. This is a prelims-relevant point.

stem: The British policy under which Indian states were annexed if a ruler died without a natural male heir (disallowing adopted heirs), a major cause of resentment, was the __________.
solution: The Doctrine of Lapse was the annexationist policy (associated especially with Lord Dalhousie) under which the British ANNEXED Indian princely states if their ruler died without a NATURAL MALE HEIR — refusing to recognise ADOPTED heirs (contrary to Indian custom). Several states (like Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur, and others) were annexed this way. This policy caused deep resentment among Indian rulers and their subjects, and grievances arising from it (e.g., the case of Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi, and Nana Sahib being denied his adoptive father's pension) fed directly into the 1857 revolt. So the policy was the Doctrine of Lapse. This is a prelims-relevant cause.

stem: The adopted son of the last Peshwa (Baji Rao II) who was denied his pension by the British and became a leader of the revolt at Kanpur (Cawnpore) was __________.
solution: Nana Sahib (Dhondu Pant) was the ADOPTED SON of the last Peshwa, Baji Rao II. After Baji Rao's death, the British REFUSED to continue his pension/titles to Nana Sahib (denying the adopted heir's claim). Aggrieved, Nana Sahib became a prominent LEADER of the revolt at Kanpur (Cawnpore) in 1857. So the leader at Kanpur was Nana Sahib. His grievance is a classic example of how British policies (denying adopted heirs) created rebel leaders. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The famous woman ruler who led the revolt at Jhansi, fighting the British after her state had been annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse, was __________.
solution: Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi was the famous woman ruler who led the revolt at Jhansi in 1857. After her husband's death, the British had ANNEXED Jhansi under the Doctrine of Lapse (refusing to recognise her adopted son as heir). She took up arms against the British, becoming one of the most celebrated leaders and symbols of the revolt, and died fighting (near Gwalior) in 1858. So the leader at Jhansi was Rani Lakshmibai. (Begum Hazrat Mahal led the revolt at Lucknow/Awadh.) This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The leader who fought the British in Awadh, defending Lucknow in the name of her young son (the deposed Nawab's heir), was __________.
solution: Begum Hazrat Mahal was a leader of the revolt in Awadh, who took up the cause of her young son Birjis Qadr (proclaiming him the ruler) after the deposed Nawab Wajid Ali Shah had been exiled by the British. She played a leading role in the rebellion at LUCKNOW (the capital of Awadh), rallying resistance against the British. So the leader defending Lucknow/Awadh was Begum Hazrat Mahal. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: Match the following 1857 rebel leaders with their centres: Nana Sahib, Rani Lakshmibai, Begum Hazrat Mahal, and Bahadur Shah Zafar were associated respectively with:
solution: The correct associations are: Nana Sahib — KANPUR (Cawnpore); Rani Lakshmibai — JHANSI; Begum Hazrat Mahal — LUCKNOW (Awadh); and Bahadur Shah Zafar — DELHI (the symbolic head of the revolt). Other important leaders included Tantia Tope (a key commander allied with Nana Sahib and later the Rani), Kunwar Singh (in Bihar/Arrah), and Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah (in Awadh). Knowing which leader was associated with which centre is prelims-relevant. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The able military commander who was a close associate of Nana Sahib (and later fought alongside the Rani of Jhansi), and who waged a prolonged guerrilla struggle, was __________.
solution: Tantia Tope (Ramchandra Panduranga) was an able military commander and a close associate/general of Nana Sahib. He played a major role in the revolt (including at Kanpur), later joined forces with Rani Lakshmibai (notably in the Gwalior campaign), and after the main centres fell he waged a prolonged GUERRILLA struggle against the British across central India before being betrayed, captured, and executed (1859). So the commander was Tantia Tope. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The rebel leader in Bihar, an elderly zamindar of Jagdishpur (Arrah), who took part in the revolt, was __________.
solution: Kunwar Singh (Kuer Singh) was an elderly zamindar of Jagdishpur (in the Arrah/Shahabad region of Bihar) who became a notable leader of the revolt in Bihar in 1857, leading rebel forces against the British despite his advanced age. He is remembered as one of the prominent leaders of the uprising. So the Bihar leader was Kunwar Singh. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The rebels sought to restore the old pre-British order. A common feature of the rebel proclamations was an appeal to __________.
options: Both Hindus and Muslims to unite against the British (invoking shared grievances and, often, the restoration of Mughal/indigenous authority)
Only one religious community, excluding all others
Foreign European powers to rule India
solution: The rebels of 1857 sought to overthrow British rule and restore the old, pre-British order (often symbolised by the restoration of Mughal/indigenous authority under Bahadur Shah Zafar). A striking feature of many rebel PROCLAMATIONS (ishtahars) was their appeal to BOTH Hindus and Muslims to UNITE against the common enemy — the British — invoking shared grievances (threats to religion, honour, livelihood, and the land) and a shared vision of expelling the foreigners. This attempt at Hindu–Muslim unity in a common cause is an important feature of the revolt's ideology. So the proclamations appealed to Hindu–Muslim unity against the British. This is a prelims-relevant point.

stem: The rebel proclamations expressed fears that British rule threatened Indians' __________.
options: Religion, caste, customs, livelihoods, and honour (a threat to their whole traditional way of life)
solution: The rebel proclamations of 1857 voiced deep FEARS that British rule threatened the very foundations of Indians' traditional way of life. They warned that the British endangered their RELIGION (through missionary activity, the cartridges, and reforms seen as attacks on faith), their CASTE and CUSTOMS, their LIVELIHOODS (through economic policies that ruined artisans, peasants, and landholders), and their HONOUR and dignity. This sense of an all-round assault on religion, society, and livelihood — a threat to their whole world (deen and dharma) — was a powerful unifying grievance mobilising diverse groups. So the proclamations expressed fears for religion, caste, customs, livelihoods, and honour. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The revolt of 1857 was ultimately __________ by the British.
options: Suppressed/crushed by 1858, with great severity and reprisals
Ignored and allowed to fizzle out peacefully
Won by the rebels but reversed later
solution: The Revolt of 1857 was ultimately SUPPRESSED/CRUSHED by the British by 1858. The British recaptured the major rebel centres (Delhi fell in September 1857; Kanpur and Lucknow were retaken; central India was subdued through 1858), often with GREAT SEVERITY — brutal reprisals, mass executions, and the destruction of towns and villages. Bahadur Shah Zafar was captured, tried, and exiled to Rangoon; leaders like the Rani of Jhansi and Tantia Tope died. So the revolt was crushed with great severity by 1858. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: A major CONSEQUENCE of the Revolt of 1857 was that __________.
options: The British Crown took over the direct governance of India from the East India Company (in 1858), ending Company rule
The Mughal Empire was restored to full power
solution: A major consequence of the Revolt of 1857 was the END of East India Company rule and the transfer of the direct governance of India to the British CROWN. By the Government of India Act of 1858, the Company was abolished and India came under the direct rule of the British Crown (with a Secretary of State for India in Britain and a Viceroy in India). Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1858) announced the new arrangements. This marked the beginning of the 'Raj' proper. So the revolt led to the Crown taking over from the Company in 1858. This is a prelims-critical fact.

stem: After 1857, the British also changed their policy toward the Indian princes and taluqdars, henceforth generally __________.
options: Reassuring them (e.g., abandoning the Doctrine of Lapse, restoring taluqdari rights in Awadh) to secure their loyalty as props of the Raj
Handing all power to the peasants
solution: After the shock of 1857, the British changed their approach toward the Indian PRINCES and TALUQDARS/landholders — the groups whose grievances had fuelled the revolt. Henceforth the British generally sought to REASSURE and CONCILIATE them to secure their loyalty as pillars/props of the Raj: they ABANDONED the Doctrine of Lapse and promised to respect the princes' rights (including adoption), and in Awadh they restored the taluqdars' estates and rights. The princes and landlords were thus cultivated as loyal allies and 'bulwarks' of British rule. So the British reassured the princes and taluqdars after 1857. This is a prelims-relevant consequence.

stem: The British also reorganised the ARMY after 1857. Which of the following changes was made?
options: The proportion of British to Indian soldiers was increased, and recruitment shifted to favour groups deemed 'loyal'/'martial'; the army was restructured to prevent another mutiny
The Indian army was completely disbanded
Only Indian officers were allowed thereafter
solution: After 1857, the British thoroughly REORGANISED the army to guard against another mutiny. Changes included: INCREASING the proportion of BRITISH (European) soldiers relative to Indian sepoys; reducing the trust placed in the groups (like the Awadh/Bengal Army sepoys) that had led the revolt, and shifting RECRUITMENT to favour communities deemed loyal and 'martial' (like Sikhs, Gurkhas, and Punjabis); mixing recruits of different castes/regions/religions in units to prevent unified solidarity; and keeping key artillery and arms firmly in British hands. So the army was restructured, with more British troops and altered recruitment, to prevent another revolt. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The chapter examines how the revolt was REPRESENTED. British visual and written representations of 1857 often __________.
options: Portrayed the British as heroic victims/avengers and the rebels as savage/villainous, to justify brutal repression and glorify the restoration of British power
Depicted the rebels as noble freedom fighters
Were entirely sympathetic to the Indian cause
solution: The chapter examines how the events of 1857 were REPRESENTED in various sources and images. BRITISH representations (paintings, prints, newspapers, memoirs, and popular literature) typically portrayed the British as HEROIC — as innocent victims of rebel 'atrocities' (especially dwelling on the killing of British women and children, e.g., at Kanpur) and as righteous AVENGERS restoring order — while depicting the REBELS as savage, treacherous, and villainous. Such representations served to JUSTIFY the brutal repression of the revolt, to rouse British public opinion, and to glorify the reassertion of British power. Historians read these images critically as constructed, partisan representations. So British representations cast the British as heroic and rebels as savage. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Later, in the nationalist imagination of India, the Revolt of 1857 came to be represented as __________.
options: The 'First War of Independence' — a heroic, patriotic struggle against foreign rule, with leaders like Rani Lakshmibai as national heroes
A minor and shameful episode to be forgotten
A purely British victory to be celebrated
An event that never really happened
solution: In the later NATIONALIST imagination, the Revolt of 1857 was re-interpreted and celebrated very differently from the British view. Indian nationalists (notably V.D. Savarkar, who called it 'The Indian War of Independence, 1857') came to represent the revolt as the 'FIRST WAR OF INDEPENDENCE' — a heroic, patriotic, and unified struggle of Indians against foreign British rule. Its leaders — Rani Lakshmibai, Nana Sahib, Tantia Tope, Bahadur Shah Zafar, and others — were exalted as NATIONAL HEROES and martyrs, inspiring the freedom movement. So nationalists represented 1857 as the First War of Independence, with its leaders as national heroes. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The different (British vs nationalist) representations of 1857 teach historians that __________.
options: Historical events are remembered and represented differently by different groups, according to their perspectives and purposes, so representations (images, texts) must themselves be analysed critically as constructed accounts
There is only one true representation, and all others are lies
Images can never be used as historical sources
The revolt has no historical importance
solution: The contrasting British and nationalist representations of 1857 teach a key methodological lesson: historical events are REMEMBERED, portrayed, and MYTHOLOGISED differently by different groups, according to their PERSPECTIVES, interests, and PURPOSES. The British cast the rebels as villains to justify repression; nationalists cast them as heroes to inspire the freedom struggle. Therefore, representations themselves — paintings, prints, memoirs, texts, and later commemorations — must be ANALYSED CRITICALLY as CONSTRUCTED accounts that reveal the viewpoint and agenda of their makers, rather than being taken as neutral, transparent records of what happened. So representations must be critically analysed as constructed. This is the chapter's central methodological theme (hence its subtitle, 'and its Representations').

stem: Assertion (A): The annexation of Awadh in 1856 was a major cause of the intensity of the 1857 revolt there. Reason (R): The annexation dispossessed the taluqdars, disrupted the social and economic order, and wounded the pride of the people by deposing the popular Nawab. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the British annexation of Awadh in 1856 was a major reason the revolt was so intense and popular there. And the reason is (R) that the annexation DISPOSSESSED the taluqdars (the powerful local landholders, whose estates and status were reduced), DISRUPTED the established social, economic, and patronage order (throwing many out of employment and unsettling revenue arrangements that hurt peasants), and WOUNDED the pride and sentiments of the people by deposing and exiling the popular Nawab Wajid Ali Shah. These grievances directly fuelled the widespread and fierce rebellion in Awadh (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): British representations of 1857 dwelt heavily on rebel 'atrocities' against British women and children. Reason (R): Such images were used to arouse public outrage in Britain and to justify severe reprisals and the reassertion of British authority. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that British representations of the revolt dwelt heavily and luridly on rebel 'atrocities' — especially the killing of British WOMEN and CHILDREN (as at Kanpur). And the reason is (R) that these emotive images and stories were deliberately used to AROUSE public OUTRAGE and a thirst for vengeance in Britain, and thereby to JUSTIFY the extremely severe REPRISALS against the rebels and the forceful reassertion of British authority in India. Presenting the British as innocent victims and the rebels as monstrous served the political purpose of legitimising brutal repression. So the propaganda purpose directly explains the emphasis on atrocities (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: Which of the following is a valid reason why 1857 is sometimes NOT called a fully 'national' movement by some historians?
options: It was largely confined to North/Central India (with major regions like the south and much of Bengal and Punjab remaining quiet), lacked a single unified leadership or a modern 'national' ideology, and involved varied local motives
It had too many leaders from the south
It was entirely a British invention
It involved no Indians at all
solution: Some historians argue that 1857, though massive, was not a fully 'NATIONAL' movement in the modern sense, for reasons such as: it was largely CONFINED to North and Central India (the Gangetic plain, Awadh, central India), while much of the SOUTH, most of BENGAL, and the PUNJAB (and many princes) remained quiet or even aided the British; it LACKED a single, unified command or a coherent MODERN nationalist ideology and programme (leadership was localised and often aimed at restoring the old pre-British order rather than creating a new nation); and participants were driven by VARIED regional, class, and personal motives rather than one common 'national' goal. (Others, and later nationalists, nonetheless see it as the first great united challenge to British rule.) So option 1 gives valid reasons. This nuance about interpretation is worth knowing.

stem: The rebels attacked and destroyed symbols of colonial authority such as __________.
options: Government offices, record rooms, treasuries, jails, police stations, and the establishments of moneylenders
solution: During the revolt, the rebels attacked and destroyed the SYMBOLS and instruments of colonial authority and oppression: government OFFICES, RECORD rooms (destroying revenue records and debt-bonds), TREASURIES (seizing money), JAILS (releasing prisoners), POLICE stations, and the courts — as well as the establishments of MONEYLENDERS (whose account-books and bonds they burnt) and other agents of the new order. This targeting reveals the rebels' grievances against the colonial administrative, fiscal, and legal apparatus and the exploitation it enabled. So they attacked government offices, records, treasuries, jails, and moneylenders' establishments. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The role of RUMOUR and PROPHECY (e.g., the greased cartridges, the passing of chapatis and lotus flowers, and the prophecy that British rule would end 100 years after Plassey) in 1857 shows that __________.
options: Rumours and prophecies helped spread fear, anticipation, and a shared sense of crisis, mobilising people — and they reflected the people's real anxieties and grievances
Rumours had no effect on the revolt
The revolt was caused only by rumours with no real grievances
solution: The 1857 revolt was accompanied by widespread RUMOURS and PROPHECIES — for example, the rumour that the greased cartridges were meant to defile Hindus and Muslims and force their conversion; the mysterious circulation of CHAPATIS and LOTUS flowers from village to village (widely interpreted as a signal or omen); and the PROPHECY that British rule would end 100 YEARS after the Battle of Plassey (1757 → 1857). Historians note that such rumours and prophecies helped SPREAD fear, anticipation, and a shared sense of impending crisis and change, MOBILISING people to act. Importantly, rumours gain force when they resonate with people's REAL anxieties and grievances — here, deep fears about threats to religion, honour, and livelihood under British rule. So rumours/prophecies helped mobilise people and reflected real anxieties. So option 1 is correct. This is an important analytical point.

stem: The Revolt of 1857 broke out during the Governor-Generalship/Viceroyalty of __________.
solution: The Revolt of 1857 broke out when Lord Canning was the Governor-General of India. After the revolt and the transfer of power to the Crown (1858), Canning became the first VICEROY of India. (Cornwallis was associated with the Permanent Settlement of 1793; Wellesley with the Subsidiary Alliance; Ripon was a later, reformist Viceroy.) So the revolt occurred under Lord Canning. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The deposed Nawab of Awadh, whose removal by the British (1856) caused great resentment and who was exiled to Calcutta, was __________.
solution: Wajid Ali Shah was the Nawab of Awadh who was deposed by the British in 1856 (on the pretext of 'misgovernment') and exiled to Calcutta. He was a popular ruler, and his removal — along with the annexation of Awadh — caused deep resentment and grief among the people and the taluqdars, contributing to the intensity of the 1857 revolt in Awadh. His young son Birjis Qadr was later proclaimed ruler by Begum Hazrat Mahal during the revolt. So the deposed Nawab was Wajid Ali Shah. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The British recaptured Delhi from the rebels in September 1857. What happened to Bahadur Shah Zafar afterwards?
options: He was captured, put on trial, and exiled to Rangoon (Burma), where he died; his sons were killed
He was restored as a powerful emperor
He escaped to Persia and ruled there
He was made Viceroy of India
solution: After the British recaptured DELHI in September 1857, the aged emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar was CAPTURED, put on TRIAL, and EXILED to Rangoon (in Burma/Myanmar), where he died in 1862. His sons (princes) were shot dead by a British officer (Hodson). This ended the Mughal dynasty and the symbolic head of the revolt. So Bahadur Shah Zafar was captured, tried, and exiled to Rangoon. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The prolonged and famous siege/struggle at Lucknow in 1857, involving the British Residency, is one of the well-known episodes of the revolt. Lucknow was the capital of __________.
solution: Lucknow was the capital of Awadh (Oudh). During the revolt, it saw a prolonged and famous struggle — including the siege of the British Residency, where the British and their supporters held out under attack by the rebels for months before being relieved. The events at Lucknow (and the Residency) became a celebrated episode in British accounts of 1857. Begum Hazrat Mahal led the rebellion in Awadh, in the name of her son Birjis Qadr. So Lucknow was the capital of Awadh. This is a prelims-relevant point.

stem: A religious leader (a maulvi) who was an influential figure in the revolt in Awadh, known for his role in the rebellion, was __________.
options: Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah (the Maulvi of Faizabad)
solution: Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah (the Maulvi of Faizabad) was an influential religious leader and preacher who became a prominent figure in the revolt of 1857 in Awadh, mobilising people and leading rebel forces against the British. He is remembered as one of the notable leaders of the uprising. (Sir Syed Ahmad Khan, by contrast, remained loyal to the British and later analysed the causes of the revolt.) So the rebel maulvi was Ahmadullah Shah of Faizabad. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The circulation of chapatis (and lotus flowers) from village to village on the eve of the revolt is significant because it __________.
options: Is interpreted as a mysterious signal/omen that spread anticipation of coming upheaval, illustrating the role of signs and rumour in the atmosphere of 1857
Was a religious festival unrelated to the revolt
Proved the revolt was purely economic
solution: On the eve of the revolt, chapatis (and, it was said, lotus flowers) were mysteriously passed from village to village and from person to person across parts of North India. Though its exact origin and meaning were unclear (even to the British, who were alarmed by it), this phenomenon has been interpreted as a mysterious SIGNAL or OMEN that spread a sense of ANTICIPATION and impending UPHEAVAL. It illustrates the charged atmosphere of 1857 and the important role of signs, rumours, and prophecies in creating a shared mood of expectation and mobilisation. So the chapati circulation is significant as a mysterious signal reflecting the role of rumour/omen. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The rebels' effort to establish some form of administration/authority in the areas they controlled (e.g., issuing orders and appointing officials in Delhi under Bahadur Shah) shows that they __________.
options: Attempted, however imperfectly, to set up a functioning alternative government and restore an ordered rule, not merely to destroy
Had no interest in governance at all
Wanted the British to keep ruling
Only wished to loot and disperse
solution: In the areas they controlled, the rebels made efforts — however imperfect and short-lived — to establish an ALTERNATIVE ADMINISTRATION and restore ordered rule. For example, in Delhi a court and administrative arrangements were set up in the name of Bahadur Shah Zafar (with a governing council, appointments, and attempts to organise the army, collect revenue, and maintain order), and similar efforts occurred at other rebel centres. This shows the rebels aimed not merely to DESTROY British rule but to RESTORE and RUN an indigenous order in its place (usually modelled on the pre-British/Mughal pattern). So they attempted to set up a functioning alternative government. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which social groups generally did NOT support the revolt (or sided with the British)?
options: Many big princes/rulers who stayed loyal, most of the south, large parts of Bengal and Punjab, the newly educated western-oriented elites, and moneylenders/merchants who often suffered rebel attacks
The sepoys of the Bengal Army
solution: Not all Indians supported the revolt; several groups stayed aloof or sided with the British. These included: many of the big PRINCES and rulers (like the Scindia of Gwalior, the Nizam of Hyderabad, and the rulers of Kashmir, Patiala, and others) who remained LOYAL to the British (indeed, their support helped the British suppress the revolt); most of SOUTHERN India and large parts of BENGAL and the PUNJAB, which stayed relatively quiet; the newly emerging WESTERN-EDUCATED elites, who by and large did not back the revolt; and the MONEYLENDERS and MERCHANTS, who were frequently TARGETS of rebel anger (their establishments attacked) and so opposed the uprising. So option 1 correctly identifies groups that did not support (or opposed) the revolt. This is a prelims-relevant point about the limits of the revolt.

stem: Historians reconstruct the rebels' own perspective on 1857 from sources such as __________.
options: Rebel proclamations (ishtahars), the depositions/statements of rebels recorded in trials and enquiries, and accounts by ordinary people — read critically alongside British records
No sources exist for the rebel viewpoint
solution: Because most detailed records were produced by the British, recovering the REBELS' own perspective is challenging, but historians use several kinds of sources: the rebel PROCLAMATIONS (ishtahars) and notices issued during the revolt; the DEPOSITIONS and statements of rebels and witnesses RECORDED in British trials, interrogations, and enquiries (which, though mediated by the colonial process, preserve rebel voices); and accounts, letters, and testimonies of ordinary people and participants. Read CRITICALLY and against the grain — alongside the British official records — these sources help reconstruct the rebels' motives, grievances, and vision. So historians use rebel proclamations and recorded depositions, read critically. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The famous British painting/print 'In Memoriam' (by Joseph Noel Paton) and images like 'The Relief of Lucknow' are examples of how art was used to __________.
options: Shape British public memory of 1857 — portraying British suffering/heroism and the rebels as threatening, thus justifying the British cause
Document the revolt with perfect neutrality
solution: British paintings and prints of 1857 — such as 'In Memoriam' (depicting helpless British women and children awaiting the rebels' onslaught) and 'The Relief of Lucknow' (celebrating the British rescue) — are examples of how ART and visual imagery were used to SHAPE British PUBLIC MEMORY and opinion of the revolt. They portrayed British innocence, SUFFERING, and HEROISM, and cast the rebels as a menacing, savage threat — thereby stirring sympathy and outrage, JUSTIFYING the British cause and the harsh repression, and glorifying the restoration of British power. Historians analyse such images as CONSTRUCTED, partisan representations rather than neutral records. So these images shaped British memory to justify the British cause. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The heavy participation of the sepoys of the Bengal Army in the revolt was partly rooted in grievances specific to them, such as __________.
options: Resentment over pay and allowances, fears about caste and religion (e.g., overseas service and the cartridges), and discontent at their treatment by British officers
solution: The sepoys of the Bengal Army (many of whom were high-caste recruits from the Awadh–Bihar region) had accumulated specific GRIEVANCES that made them central to the revolt. These included: resentment over PAY, allowances, and conditions of service (e.g., disputes over batta/allowances and postings); fears about CASTE and RELIGION — such as the General Service Enlistment requirement to serve OVERSEAS (crossing the sea was seen as caste-polluting), and above all the greased CARTRIDGES; and discontent at their harsh, discriminatory TREATMENT by British officers (loss of the older, more paternal bonds; racism; blocked promotions). Their grievances were also linked to those of the rural society (Awadh) from which they came. So the sepoys' grievances included pay, caste/religious fears, and mistreatment. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The revolt is significant in the long run because, even though it failed, it __________.
options: Shook the foundations of British rule, forced major changes in colonial policy and administration, and became a powerful source of inspiration and symbolism for the later national/freedom movement
Made no difference to Indian history
Permanently ended all resistance to the British
Caused Indians to welcome British rule
solution: Although the Revolt of 1857 ultimately FAILED (it was crushed by 1858), it was highly significant in the long run. It profoundly SHOOK the foundations of British rule and demonstrated the depth of Indian discontent; it FORCED major CHANGES in colonial policy and administration (the transfer of power from Company to Crown; the conciliation of princes and landlords; the reorganisation of the army; a more cautious approach to social/religious interference); and it became a powerful SOURCE of INSPIRATION and SYMBOLISM for later generations of Indian nationalists — the memory of 1857 and its heroes (recast as the 'First War of Independence') helped inspire the freedom struggle. So the revolt, though it failed, had lasting impact and inspirational value. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The revolt's attempt to unite Hindus and Muslims (under a Mughal symbol, with appeals to both communities) is historically notable because it __________.
options: Demonstrated a shared opposition to British rule that cut across religious lines, an important precedent later invoked in the nationalist movement
Proved the two communities could never cooperate
solution: The Revolt of 1857 is historically notable for its attempt at HINDU–MUSLIM UNITY: the rebellion rallied around the Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar as a shared symbol, and the rebel proclamations appealed to BOTH Hindus and Muslims to unite against the common British enemy (invoking shared threats to religion, honour, and livelihood). Hindus and Muslims fought side by side in many places. This demonstrated a SHARED OPPOSITION to British rule that CUT ACROSS religious lines — an important precedent and inspiration that was later invoked in the nationalist movement's ideal of communal unity in the freedom struggle. So the Hindu–Muslim cooperation in 1857 is notable as a cross-communal opposition to British rule. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following is the correct chronological sequence of events?
options: Barrackpore (Mangal Pandey, March 1857) → Meerut mutiny (10 May 1857) → march to Delhi/proclamation of Bahadur Shah → fall of Delhi (Sept 1857) → suppression by 1858 → Crown takes over (1858)
Crown takes over → Meerut mutiny → Barrackpore → fall of Delhi
Fall of Delhi → Meerut mutiny → Barrackpore → Crown takes over
Meerut mutiny → Crown takes over → Barrackpore → fall of Delhi
solution: The correct chronological sequence is: Mangal Pandey's defiance at BARRACKPORE (late March 1857) → the outbreak of the mutiny at MEERUT (10 May 1857) → the sepoys' march to DELHI and the proclamation of Bahadur Shah Zafar as leader (May 1857) → the British recapture/FALL of DELHI (September 1857) → the general SUPPRESSION of the revolt by 1858 → the transfer of power from the East India Company to the British CROWN (Government of India Act, 1858; Queen's Proclamation). Knowing this sequence is prelims-relevant. So option 1 gives the correct order.

stem: The British reprisals after the revolt were often extremely harsh, including __________.
options: Mass executions of rebels and suspected sympathisers (sometimes by hanging or being 'blown from cannon'), and the destruction of towns/villages
solution: The British suppression of the revolt was accompanied by extremely HARSH reprisals and reprisal-driven violence. These included MASS EXECUTIONS of captured rebels and suspected sympathisers — many were hanged, and some were executed by the terrifying method of being 'blown from cannon' (tied to the mouth of a cannon and blasted apart) — as well as the burning and DESTRUCTION of towns and villages associated with the revolt, and indiscriminate killing during the recapture of centres like Delhi. These brutal reprisals were meant to punish, terrorise, and deter, and they left a bitter legacy. So the reprisals included mass executions and destruction of settlements. This underscores the severity of the repression.

stem: The chapter's title includes 'and its Representations' primarily to signal that the chapter also studies __________.
options: How the revolt was portrayed, remembered, and imagined (in British and nationalist images, texts, and memory) — not just what happened
The representation of Indians in Parliament
solution: The phrase 'and its Representations' in the chapter's title signals that the chapter studies not only the EVENTS of 1857 (what happened) but also — importantly — how the revolt was PORTRAYED, REMEMBERED, and IMAGINED in various REPRESENTATIONS: British paintings, prints, newspapers, and memoirs (casting the British as heroic victims and the rebels as savages), and later Indian nationalist writings and images (celebrating 1857 as the First War of Independence and its leaders as heroes). Analysing these representations critically — as constructed accounts shaped by the makers' viewpoints and purposes — is a central concern of the chapter. So the title points to the study of how the revolt was represented and remembered. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): After 1857, the British increased the proportion of European soldiers and changed recruitment patterns in the army. Reason (R): They wanted to reduce the risk of another large-scale mutiny by making the army more reliable and harder to unite in rebellion. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that after 1857 the British increased the proportion of EUROPEAN (British) soldiers relative to Indian sepoys and changed RECRUITMENT patterns (favouring communities deemed loyal/'martial', and mixing castes, regions, and religions within units). And the reason is (R) that they did this precisely to REDUCE the risk of ANOTHER large-scale MUTINY — making the army more reliable and controllable, and harder for the soldiers to UNITE in a common rebellion (by diluting shared caste/regional solidarity and keeping firmer British control over arms and key units). So the aim of preventing another mutiny directly explains the army changes (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): The Revolt of 1857 is remembered as both a 'sepoy mutiny' and a 'war of independence'. Reason (R): Different observers and later commentators, with different perspectives and purposes, interpreted and named the same event in different ways. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the events of 1857 have been remembered and NAMED in very different ways — as a mere 'Sepoy Mutiny' (the British/colonial label, stressing a military revolt), and as the 'First War of Independence' (the nationalist label, stressing a patriotic national uprising), among other characterisations. And the reason is (R) that DIFFERENT observers and later commentators — the British, the nationalists, various historians — approached the event with DIFFERENT perspectives, interests, and PURPOSES, and therefore interpreted, framed, and named it differently. So the diversity of perspectives directly explains the differing names/interpretations (A). So R correctly explains A. This captures the chapter's theme about representations.

stem: The taluqdars of Awadh were important to the revolt because they __________.
options: Were powerful local landholders with armed retainers and influence over the peasantry, so their disaffection (after being stripped of their estates on annexation) helped mobilise widespread rural rebellion
solution: The taluqdars of Awadh were POWERFUL local LANDHOLDERS/magnates, with substantial estates, ARMED RETAINERS (their own troops and forts), and deep INFLUENCE over the peasantry and rural society. When the British ANNEXED Awadh (1856) and, in the ensuing revenue settlement, STRIPPED many taluqdars of their estates and reduced their power and status, these influential figures became deeply DISAFFECTED. Their disaffection was crucial to the revolt in Awadh: commanding local loyalty and armed followers, the taluqdars could and did MOBILISE widespread rural rebellion against the British. (After the revolt, the British reversed course and restored the taluqdars to win their loyalty.) So the taluqdars' disaffection helped mobilise the rebellion. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A key reason the revolt spread so rapidly once it began was that __________.
options: Shared grievances and networks (among sepoys and across rural society) meant that news of the Meerut/Delhi uprising quickly inspired risings elsewhere, as many were already primed to revolt
The British encouraged it to spread
There were no communications at all
Only one town was ever involved
solution: The revolt spread rapidly once it began because SHARED GRIEVANCES and NETWORKS had already PRIMED many people — sepoys and rural society alike — to rise. The sepoys across North India shared common discontents (the cartridges, service conditions, caste/religious fears) and were linked by networks of communication and kinship; and the wider rural society harboured deep grievances (annexations, revenue burdens, threats to religion and livelihood). So when NEWS of the Meerut mutiny and the seizure of Delhi (and the proclamation of Bahadur Shah) spread, it acted as a SIGNAL that quickly INSPIRED further risings elsewhere — sepoys mutinied at station after station, and civilians joined in — because so many were already ready to revolt. So option 1 is correct — shared grievances and networks enabled rapid spread.

stem: Which statement best captures the chapter's approach to studying 1857?
options: It only lists dates and battles

It combines the reconstruction of what happened (causes, course, leaders, consequences) with a critical analysis of the SOURCES and REPRESENTATIONS (both British and Indian), teaching students to weigh perspectives and read images and texts critically
It relies solely on British accounts uncritically
It avoids all discussion of causes
solution: The chapter's approach COMBINES two things: (1) the RECONSTRUCTION of the revolt itself — its causes (the cartridges, annexations, the Doctrine of Lapse, agrarian and social grievances, threats to religion), its course (Meerut, Delhi, the major centres and leaders), and its consequences (suppression, the transfer to Crown rule, policy and army changes); and (2) a CRITICAL ANALYSIS of the SOURCES and REPRESENTATIONS through which 1857 is known and remembered — both British (portraying rebels as savages, to justify repression) and Indian/nationalist (celebrating the First War of Independence). In doing so, it TEACHES students to weigh different perspectives and to read images, proclamations, memoirs, and texts CRITICALLY. So option 2 best captures the chapter's approach.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Rebels and the Raj: The Revolt of 1857 and its Representations' is that:
options: The Revolt of 1857 was an insignificant local mutiny with no causes or consequences

The Revolt of 1857 was a massive uprising — beginning with the sepoys at Meerut and spreading (especially across North and Central India, with centres at Delhi under Bahadur Shah Zafar, Kanpur under Nana Sahib, Jhansi under Rani Lakshmibai, and Lucknow under Begum Hazrat Mahal) into a broad popular rebellion of sepoys, peasants, artisans, and dispossessed landholders, driven by deep grievances (over cartridges, annexations like Awadh and the Doctrine of Lapse, and threats to religion, livelihood, and honour) and a vision of restoring the old order and uniting Hindus and Muslims against the British; though crushed with great severity by 1858, it led to the transfer of power from the Company to the Crown and major changes in policy and the army — and its memory has been represented very differently by the British (as savage rebellion) and by nationalists (as the First War of Independence), so these representations must themselves be read critically
1857 was purely a British victory to be celebrated
The revolt had no leaders and no popular support
solution: The chapter's overall message is that the Revolt of 1857 was a MASSIVE and momentous uprising against British/Company rule. It began with the mutiny of the sepoys at Meerut (10 May 1857) — sparked immediately by the greased-cartridge affair — and spread rapidly, especially across NORTH and CENTRAL India, becoming a BROAD POPULAR rebellion that drew in sepoys, peasants, artisans, and dispossessed taluqdars/landholders. It rallied around symbols of the old order, proclaiming the Mughal emperor BAHADUR SHAH ZAFAR at Delhi as its head, with major centres and leaders including NANA SAHIB at Kanpur, RANI LAKSHMIBAI at Jhansi, BEGUM HAZRAT MAHAL at Lucknow (Awadh), and others like Tantia Tope and Kunwar Singh. The revolt was driven by DEEP and varied GRIEVANCES — the cartridges and threats to religion and caste; annexations and dispossession (the Doctrine of Lapse, and the resented annexation of Awadh); the ruin of livelihoods; and wounded honour — and by a VISION of expelling the British, restoring indigenous authority, and uniting Hindus and Muslims in a common cause (as expressed in the rebel proclamations, and spread by rumour and prophecy). Though the British ultimately CRUSHED it with great severity by 1858, it had far-reaching CONSEQUENCES: the abolition of Company rule and the transfer of power to the British CROWN (1858), and major changes in policy (conciliating princes and taluqdars, abandoning the Doctrine of Lapse) and in the ARMY. Finally, the chapter stresses that the revolt has been REPRESENTED very differently — by the British as a savage, treacherous rebellion (to justify repression) and by Indian nationalists as the heroic 'First War of Independence' — so these representations (images and texts) must themselves be read CRITICALLY as constructed accounts. So the overall message is option 2.
